summary: The article explains alternative investment avenues for India's growing population of high-net-worth investors (HNIs): Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), Portfolio Management Services (PMS) and Market-linked Debentures (MLDs). It describes how each works, minimum investment thresholds and the types of AIF strategies, arguing these products offer diversification and low correlation with traditional assets. It closes by advising research, checking track records and consulting knowledgeable advisors.
one_line: Overview of AIFs, PMS and market-linked debentures as alternative investments for India's rapidly growing high-net-worth investor population.
key_facts: India's HNI population (assets of $1 million or more) was 7.9 lakh in 2022 and is projected to rise to 16.5 lakh in five years, a 107 per cent increase.
AIFs were launched in 2012 after SEBI issued guidelines for their management, and are divided into Categories I, II and III.
AIFs have a minimum investment of ₹1 crore, which can be collected in tranches called drawdowns over 2-3 years.
AIFs have amassed an AUM of ₹8.30-lakh crore in the 11 years since their inception.
AIF returns are generally uncorrelated with publicly traded equity or debt markets, offering a natural hedge against volatility.

AIF types listed include start-up funds, mid-stage PE funds, late-stage/pre-IPO funds, hedge funds, performing credit funds, infrastructure funds and venture debt funds; others include special situation funds and real estate yield funds.
Pre-IPO funds gained immense popularity after the 2020 stock market rally that saw blockbuster listings of popular B2C company IPOs.
Infrastructure funds invest in assets such as roads, power transmission lines and solar power plants, generating annuity-backed cashflows distributed regularly to investors.
PMS guidelines in India date back to 1993; PMS AUM (excluding EPFO/PF) stood at ₹5.28 lakh crore as of July 2023, with a minimum investment of ₹50 lakh.
In PMS, beneficial ownership of securities lies with the investor rather than the fund, and PMS comes in discretionary and non-discretionary options.
Market-linked debentures are non-convertible debt instruments tied to benchmarks such as the Nifty 50, the BSE Sensex or the 10-year G-Sec, with maturities of one to five years.
MLDs have a minimum investment of ₹1 lakh but are more popular with HNIs due to their complex structure, and they pay no periodic interest before maturity.
Equity-linked MLDs commonly feature income multipliers and principal protection up to the debenture's face value.
The author is President & Head, Nuvama Wealth.
